content: The hypothesis of the vicious cycle in bronchiectasis suggests that bacterial colonization of the respiratory tract leads to persistent inflammation. This inflammation damages the mucociliary escalator, impairing the clearance of bacteria and allowing pro-inflammatory mediators to persist. Conventional treatments, such as physiotherapy and intermittent antibiotics, are thought to improve the condition of individuals with bronchiectasis, but there is no definitive evidence that these interventions alter the natural progression of the disease. To disrupt this cycle of infection and inflammation, one strategy has been to extend the duration of antibiotic therapy, with the aim of promoting healing of the airway mucosa. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits of prolonged antibiotic therapy in managing bronchiectasis. A systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group Trials Register and reference lists of relevant articles, with searches updated as of February 2014. Randomized controlled trials that compared prolonged antibiotic therapy (lasting four or more weeks) to placebo or standard care were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, contacting study authors when necessary to obtain missing information. Eighteen trials met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 1,157 participants. The duration of antibiotic treatment ranged from four weeks to 83 weeks. Due to variability in reported outcomes, only limited meta-analysis was feasible. Based on the number of participants experiencing at least one exacerbation, the meta-analysis demonstrated a significant benefit of prolonged antibiotic therapy. The odds ratio (OR) for experiencing an exacerbation was 0.31 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.52; P < 0.00001), indicating a substantial reduction in exacerbations. Specifically, 271 per 1,000 people in the intervention group experienced exacerbations (95% CI 126 to 385), compared to 546 per 1,000 in the control group. The evidence supporting this finding was of moderate quality. Although there was a trend toward reduced hospitalizations in the prolonged antibiotic group, this finding was not statistically significant. Hospitalization rates were 37 per 1,000 in the intervention group (95% CI 13 to 96) compared to 87 per 1,000 in the control group (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.11; P = 0.08). The evidence supporting this outcome was also of moderate quality. However, the use of prolonged antibiotics was associated with an increased risk of developing drug resistance. Resistance was observed in 36 of 220 participants receiving antibiotics, compared to 10 of 211 participants in the placebo or standard care group (OR 3.48, 95% CI 1.20 to 10.07; P = 0.02). This corresponds to 155 cases of drug resistance per 1,000 people in the intervention group (95% CI 59 to 346), compared to 50 cases per 1,000 in the control group. The intervention was generally well tolerated, with no significant difference in withdrawal rates between the antibiotic and placebo groups (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.49). Diarrhea was a commonly reported adverse event, particularly with oral antibiotic regimens. In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that prolonged antibiotic therapy provides significant benefits for patients with bronchiectasis, reducing the odds of exacerbations by at least half and potentially lowering hospitalization rates. For every 1,000 people treated with prolonged antibiotics, there were 275 fewer exacerbations and 50 fewer hospitalizations compared to the control group. However, this benefit comes with a more than threefold increase in the risk of developing drug resistance. The findings of this review are limited by the heterogeneity of the included trials and the moderate to low quality of the evidence. Further randomized controlled trials with sufficient power and standardized endpoints are needed to confirm these results.
